procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Special Judge appointed under the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952, Greater Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Special Judge tendering a conditional pardon to a co-accused (Jagasia) and ordering that he be examined as an approver and witness for the prosecution.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Fernandes) filed a criminal revision application in the Bombay High Court challenging the Special Judge's order. The High Court dismissed the revision application, upholding the tender of conditional pardon to Jagasia.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (Fernandes) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the Bombay High Court's order. The appellant contended that the Special Judge's power to tender pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act is limited to applications by the prosecution and that the Special Judge's discretion was not exercised judicially or properly.

issue.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge in tendering pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are limited to an application by the prosecution, or if the Judge can act suo motu.

facts: A clerk, who was a co-accused in a corruption case, applied to the Special Judge to be made an approver (a witness for the prosecution).
The other co-accused, including the appellant, opposed this application.
The Special Judge, acting under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, tendered a pardon to the clerk.
The appellant argued that the Special Judge could not do this without an application from the prosecution, i.e., the judge could not act 'suo motu' (on his own initiative).
law: The issue revolves around the interpretation of a Special Judge's power to tender a pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act.
The appellant's argument was based on a comparison of s. 8(2) with ss. 337 and 338 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), which also deal with tendering pardons.
Section 8(2) states that a pardon tendered by a Special Judge is 'deemed' to be a pardon under s. 338 Cr.P.C. for the purposes of applying ss. 339 and 339A.
application: The appellant contended that the differences between the powers of a Special Judge under the Act and the powers of other courts under the Cr.P.C. showed that the Special Judge's power was limited and could only be exercised if the prosecution moved an application first.

The Court examined the differences between the sections. It noted that the 'deeming' provision in s. 8(2) was limited in scope; it only meant that the consequences of a pardon (as laid out in ss. 339 and 339A of the Cr.P.C.) would apply. It did not mean the entire procedure of s. 338 was applicable.

The Court acknowledged other differences, such as the fact that a Special Judge cannot order a committing magistrate to tender a pardon because there is no commitment proceeding in a trial before a Special Judge.

However, the Court reasoned that these procedural differences do not lead to the conclusion that the Special Judge's fundamental power to tender a pardon is restricted. The text states that these differences "do not, howe'1er, show that the powers of the [Special Judge are limited]".
By rejecting the appellant's reasoning, the Court implicitly affirmed that the power is not limited to an application by the prosecution.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention. It held that the procedural differences between s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act and ss. 337/338 of the Cr.P.C. do not mean that the Special Judge's power to tender a pardon is limited to an application by the prosecution. Therefore, the Judge can act suo motu.

issue.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are circumscribed by the considerations underlying s. 540 Cr. P. C., and therefore he could not acquit one accused so as to be able to convict another.

law.fact_text: Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) confers power on a court to summon material witnesses at any stage of an inquiry, trial, or other proceeding.
Section 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act grants a Special Judge the power to tender a pardon to an accused person.

application.fact_text: The Supreme Court held that there was no merit in the contention that Section 540 Cr.P.C. governs the power to tender a pardon under Section 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act.
The Court reasoned that the power to summon witnesses under s. 540 is not to be confused with the power to tender a pardon to an accused.
It explained that the considerations for summoning a court witness are "somewhat different" from the considerations for tendering a pardon.
While both actions must be taken in the interests of justice, the Court stated that this is where the "common factor ceases and other considerations arise."

reasoning.conclusion: The Court concluded that it is not possible to read Section 540 Cr.P.C. together with Section 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act. Therefore, the Special Judge's power to tender a pardon (which may result in one accused being acquitted to help convict another) is not circumscribed by the considerations underlying the power to summon witnesses.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge had exercised his discretion judicially and properly in tendering the pardon.

facts: An accused clerk in a corruption trial applied directly to the Special Judge to be granted a pardon and become a prosecution witness (an approver).
The Special Judge, acting on his own initiative ('suo motu'), granted the conditional pardon without first consulting the prosecution.
The case was appealed to the High Court, where the Public Prosecutor stated that the prosecution welcomed and favourably considered the tender of pardon to the clerk.
law: Before tendering a pardon, a judge must know the nature of the evidence the person is likely to give and their degree of culpability compared to the other co-accused.
Ordinarily, it is for the prosecution to request that an accused be tendered a pardon.

If an accused applies directly to the judge, the proper course is for the judge to first refer the request to the prosecution for its opinion. The judge should not take it upon themselves to decide the matter without the prosecution's input.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Special Judge had acted improperly.
The Judge failed to follow the correct procedure by not first asking for the prosecution's opinion on the clerk's application.
Furthermore, the Judge made no effort to find out what evidence the clerk intended to disclose before granting the pardon.
The Court stated that the practice of a judge tendering a pardon 'suo motu' at the request of an accused is to be avoided.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Special Judge had not exercised his discretion judicially or properly. However, the Court chose not to interfere with the order and dismissed the appeal. The reason for this was that the prosecution had subsequently stated in the High Court that it supported the decision to grant the pardon. Since the prosecution ultimately wanted the pardon to be tendered, the Court allowed it to stand despite the procedural errors made by the Special Judge.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge in tendering pardon under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are limited to an application by the prosecution, or if the Judge can act suo motu.
appellant_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge in tendering a pardon under s. 8(2) are limited to an application by the prosecution.
The Special Judge cannot act suo motu (on his own initiative) without being invited by the prosecution to consider tendering a pardon.
respondent_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge to grant a pardon are untrammelled and not conditioned by the considerations the appellant relies on.
There is nothing in the section to show that the Special Judge must be moved by the prosecution; he may consider an offer by an accused, and such action is within his jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the powers of the Special Judge under s. 8(2) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act are circumscribed by the considerations underlying s. 540 Cr. P. C., and therefore he could not acquit one accused so as to be able to convict another.
appellant_arguments: The Special Judge's powers under s. 8(2) are circumscribed by the considerations that underlie s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Judge can only act in the interests of justice and not with the view of acquitting one accused just to be able to convict another.
respondent_arguments: The powers of the Special Judge to grant pardon are untrammelled.

The sections in both the Code and the Criminal Law Amendment Act related to tendering a pardon to secure evidence are not conditioned by the considerations the appellant relies on (such as those in s. 540 Cr. P. C.).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Special Judge had exercised his discretion judicially and properly in tendering the pardon.
appellant_arguments: The Special Judge did not exercise his discretion judicially or properly.
Before tendering a pardon, the Judge must know the nature of the evidence the person will give, their complicity, and their culpability relative to the other co-accused.
In this case, the Special Judge made no effort to find out what the applicant (Jagasia) had to disclose.
respondent_arguments: The pardon was justified because the person receiving it (Jagasia) is an insignificant person compared to the contractors and superior officers who are mainly responsible for defrauding the Government.
The prosecution stated in the High Court that it had no objection to the pardon and welcomed the opportunity to have an approver's evidence.

cases.principle: The provided text does not state the legal principle for which this case was cited.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Although the statutory power of a Special Judge to tender a pardon is wide and can be initiated upon an application by an accused, this power must be exercised on behalf of the prosecuting agency and only when the prosecution joins in the request. A Special Judge must not independently determine the propriety of tendering a pardon but must first refer the accused's request to the prosecution for its opinion.
obiter: Ordinarily, it is for the prosecution to ask that a particular accused be tendered a pardon.
The prosecution may not want to tender a pardon to the principal offender or the worst offender.
If the prosecution believes the tender of pardon is in the interest of a successful prosecution, it will likely agree.
The practice of a judge tendering a pardon suo motu at the request of an accused is to be avoided.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While a Special Judge acts improperly by tendering a pardon suo motu at an accused's request without first consulting the prosecution, this procedural error is cured if the prosecution subsequently supports the pardon. The power to tender a pardon is distinct from and not circumscribed by the considerations for summoning witnesses under s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
legal_tests_applied: When an accused directly applies for a pardon, the proper course for the Special Judge is to first refer the request to the prosecuting agency for its opinion, as the power is exercised on behalf of the prosecution.

Before tendering a pardon, the Judge must know the nature of the evidence the person is likely to give, the nature of their complicity, and the degree of their culpability in relation to the offence and the other co-accused.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the power to pardon under s. 8(2) is governed by s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was rejected, as the court found the power to summon witnesses is distinct from the power to tender a pardon, and the considerations for each are different.

Although the court agreed that the Special Judge acted improperly by not consulting the prosecution, the appeal was dismissed because the Public Prosecutor later stated in the High Court that the prosecution supported the tender of pardon, which cured the initial procedural defect.
why_respondent_won: The court held that the sections of law concerning the tender of a pardon are not conditioned by the considerations underlying s. 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The respondent ultimately prevailed because the prosecution's subsequent approval of the pardon in the High Court was deemed sufficient for the Supreme Court to decline interference, despite the Special Judge's flawed initial procedure.
policy_considerations: The interests of the accused are just as important as those of the prosecution, and no procedure or action can be in the interest of justice if it is prejudicial to an accused.

It is not for the Special Judge to enter the ring as a veritable director of prosecution; the power to pardon is exercised on behalf of the prosecuting agency, which may have strategic reasons to oppose it, such as not wanting to pardon the worst offender.
The court cautioned that the practice of a Judge tendering a pardon suo motu at the request of an accused is to be avoided.
